# Settings

<!-- Generated by `uv run poe gen` from src/config.py. Do not edit by hand. -->

Every setting the application reads, as declared in `src/config.py`. Each is
set through the environment or `.env` under its upper-case name; `.env.example`
lists them all (enforced by ARCH-ENVEX). Defaults are shown as written in the
source. The description is the comment above the field, the field's
`description`, or the docstring under it.

## LLM (Groq)

| Variable | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `GROQ_API_KEY` | `str` | `""` |  |
| `GROQ_CHAT_MODEL` | `str` | `"openai/gpt-oss-120b"` | Used for extraction, drafting and review. |
| `GROQ_REASONING_FORMAT` | `Literal["parsed", "hidden", "raw", ""]` | `"parsed"` | Groq's reasoning_format: parsed, hidden, raw, or '' to send nothing |
| `GROQ_BASE_URL` | `str \| None` | `"https://api.me-central-1.groqcloud.com"` | ME-Central-1 regional endpoint. Host root only — the groq client appends `/openai/v1` to it. Set to "" to fall back to the global api.groq.com. |
| `LLM_TEMPERATURE` | `float` | `0.0` |  |
| `EVAL_JUDGE_MODEL` | `str` | `"openai/gpt-oss-120b"` | Grading model for eval/. Deliberately not the drafting model: a system should not mark its own homework. |

## Tracing (LangSmith)

| Variable | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `LANGSMITH_TRACING` | `bool` | `False` | Every LLM call, retrieval and graph step recorded as a trace. Off unless deliberately switched on, and the reason is data residency rather than cost. A trace carries the prompt, and the prompt carries the policy chunks retrieved to answer the question. LangSmith has no Saudi region -- `langsmith_endpoint` chooses between the EU and the US -- so enabling this transfers internal policy text, and the client questionnaires being answered, outside Saudi Arabia. That is a decision for whoever owns the documents, not a default worth inheriting. |
| `LANGSMITH_ENDPOINT` | `str` | `"https://eu.api.smith.langchain.com"` |  |
| `LANGSMITH_API_KEY` | `str` | `""` |  |
| `LANGSMITH_PROJECT` | `str` | `"Cyber-Assessment-Answering-Agent"` |  |

## Tracing (Phoenix, on this machine)

| Variable | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `PHOENIX_TRACING` | `bool` | `False` | The same traces, kept locally. Phoenix is an OpenTelemetry collector with a UI that understands LLM spans, and it runs wherever this does, so the data-residency objection to LangSmith does not apply: nothing crosses a border, or leaves the host at all. Still off by default, because a trace is a copy of the policy text and the customer's questionnaire in a second store with no access control in front of it. Local is not the same as harmless -- see docs/operations/tracing.md. |
| `PHOENIX_ENDPOINT` | `str` | `"http://localhost:6006/v1/traces"` |  |
| `PHOENIX_PROJECT` | `str` | `"assessment-answer"` |  |

## Embeddings (BGE-M3 behind an OpenAI-compatible endpoint)

| Variable | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `EMBEDDING_BASE_URL` | `str` | `"https://ds.t2.sa/text_embed/v1"` |  |
| `EMBEDDING_MODEL` | `str` | `"bge-m3"` |  |
| `EMBEDDING_API_KEY` | `str` | `"unused"` |  |
| `EMBEDDING_TIMEOUT` | `float` | `300.0` | Seconds one embedding request may take before it is retried (twice) and then fails. Ingestion sends 64 chunks per request, so this bounds one batch, not a whole file. Without it the client waited for ever: a stalled host held a run for 53 minutes (TD-034, plan 017). |

## Document conversion (Docling)

| Variable | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `DOCLING_BASE_URL` | `str` | `"http://localhost:8092"` | Docling runs as a container on the testing server and converts PDF/DOCX to Markdown. Host root only — the endpoint paths are appended. Set to "" to skip it entirely and use the local pdfplumber / python-docx loaders. |
| `DOCLING_TIMEOUT` | `float` | `180.0` | Per-HTTP-request timeout: submitting a file, polling a task, fetching a result. Each is short; the conversion itself is not one request. |
| `DOCLING_CONVERSION_TIMEOUT` | `float` | `2400.0` | Total budget for one document's conversion, across all the polls it takes. A 161-page standard runs well past the 300s cap the Docling server puts on synchronous requests, which is why conversion is submitted asynchronously. |
| `DOCLING_DO_OCR` | `bool` | `False` | Force OCR on every document. Off by default: on a born-digital PDF it costs ~2.3x and adds only whatever text sits inside the logos, while table structure comes from a separate model that runs regardless. |
| `DOCLING_OCR_AUTO` | `bool` | `True` | Turn OCR on automatically for a PDF with no usable text layer, so a scanned upload is still read without making OCR everyone's default. |
| `DOCLING_IMAGE_EXPORT_MODE` | `Literal["placeholder", "embedded", "referenced"]` | `"placeholder"` |  |
| `DOCLING_PAGE_BREAK_PLACEHOLDER` | `str` | `"<!-- docling-page-break -->"` | Docling emits Markdown with no page information at all, so a citation could name a clause but never a page. Given a placeholder it inserts one between pages, which `docling_client` then rewrites into the numbered markers the chunker already understands. Something that cannot occur in a policy: it is matched literally. |
| `DOCLING_HEADING_HIERARCHY` | `bool` | `True` | Build a real heading hierarchy from bookmarks, numbering and styles. Off in Docling by default, and the consequence is severe here: 85 of 86 documents came back with every heading at one level, which leaves the chunker a flat list where it expects a tree. A chapter with no sub-levels cannot be divided by its own subsections, which is how this corpus ended up with units of 40, 100 and 113 parts. See src/chunking.py. |
| `DOCLING_FALLBACK_LOCAL` | `bool` | `True` | When Docling is unreachable, fall back to the local loaders rather than failing the upload. Set false to make a broken Docling loud instead. |

## Reading questionnaires

| Variable | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `DETECTION_STRATEGY` | `Literal["rules", "assisted", "agent", "hybrid", "guarded"]` | `"guarded"` | How hard to work at understanding an uploaded questionnaire: 'rules', 'assisted', 'agent', 'hybrid' or 'guarded'. Described, measured and compared in `src.forms.reading`. 'guarded' by default -- the agent, floored by the rules. Measured over six questionnaires in shapes nobody had written a rule for, the agent read 292 of 292 against the rules' 272; measured over the nineteen we already had, it quietly dropped a whole sheet. Running both and taking the better reading per sheet costs one deterministic pass on top of the agent, which is milliseconds and nothing. |
| `DETECTION_ASSIST` | `bool` | `False` | A sheet the rules cannot read is offered to a model, which proposes a layout the ordinary reader then extracts from -- see `forms.llm_layout`. Off by default: the rules read every sample workbook we have, so this costs a call per unreadable sheet for files we have not seen yet. The 'assisted' strategy turns it on for one reading without changing this. |
| `DETECTION_ASSIST_COVERAGE` | `float` | `0.25` | A sheet where the rules found questions on fewer than this share of the rows below the header is also offered, because "7 questions on a sheet of 133 rows" is a wrong column rather than a short questionnaire. The model's reading is taken only if it finds more, so assistance can add questions but never remove them. |
| `DETECTION_ASSIST_MIN_ROWS` | `int` | `20` |  |
| `EXCEL_AGENT_MAX_STEPS` | `int` | `24` | The Excel agent reads a workbook through tools instead, exploring it before committing to a layout. Built to be compared against the two above rather than to replace them; see `src.agents.excel_agent`. |

## Retrieval + answering

| Variable | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `TOP_K_GUIDELINES` | `int` | `8` | Guideline chunks retrieved per search query. |
| `TOP_K_PRIOR_ANSWERS` | `int` | `5` | Previous answers retrieved per question. |
| `QUERY_EXPANSION` | `bool` | `True` | Split a multi-part question into one search per part before retrieving. Costs one extra LLM call per question; turn it off to retrieve on the question's own wording alone. |
| `MAX_SEARCH_QUERIES` | `int` | `6` | The verbatim question always occupies the first slot, so this is one more than the number of decomposed angles. Four left only three angles for a question needing five different policies, which is most of what multi-document recall was losing. |
| `HYBRID_SEARCH` | `bool` | `False` | Fuse a BM25 pass with the dense search, to catch the exact figures embeddings blur — "72 hours", "90 days", "12 characters". Off by default because it measured worse on the T2 corpus: 71.4% against 73.6% for dense alone. It does what it claims (it moved the PDPL 72-hour clause from rank 11 to rank 1) but it also promotes the wrong section of the right document, and on the golden set it lost more than it won. Turn it on for a corpus whose questions are mostly exact-figure lookups, and re-run `eval/` to check. See src/lexical.py. |
| `LEXICAL_WEIGHT` | `float` | `0.4` | How much the BM25 ranking counts against the dense one. Below 1.0 it can promote a chunk dense also found but ranked low, without letting a keyword-only match displace a semantically better hit. |
| `RERANKER_ENABLED` | `bool` | `False` | Cross-encoder reranking of the retrieved evidence, once per question. See src/rerank.py; the model is downloaded on first use (~2.3 GB). |
| `RERANKER_MODEL` | `str` | `"BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3"` |  |
| `RERANKER_MAX_LENGTH` | `int` | `1024` |  |
| `RERANKER_BATCH_SIZE` | `int` | `16` |  |
| `MAX_ANSWER_ATTEMPTS` | `int` | `3` | Draft/review rounds per question. Evidence accumulates across rounds rather than being replaced, so a third attempt adds material to the drafter's context instead of trading one retrieval for another. |
| `MAX_CONCURRENT_QUESTIONS` | `int` | `4` | Questions answered at once. Raise carefully: Groq rate limits apply. |
| `MAX_CONCURRENT_REWRITES` | `int` | `8` | Rewordings reaching the model at once: preferences, skills, "make them shorter", and the brief form, each one call per answer. Unbounded, 80 at once lost 44 to Groq's rate limit and every lost one stayed as it was. |
| `STORAGE_LIMIT_PER_USER_MB` | `int` | `2048` | Stored files per person: the questionnaires they uploaded and the filled copies written from them. Under the limit nothing is removed; over it, the files of the work they have not used longest go first -- never a document the team's knowledge base was built from, and never anything used in the last STORAGE_KEEP_DAYS days, whatever the limit says. Per person, because that is who a questionnaire belongs to, so a new colleague brings their own allowance. 0 turns the limit off. |
| `STORAGE_KEEP_DAYS` | `int` | `30` | Nothing used this recently is removed, even over the limit. |
| `REVIEW_CONFIDENCE_THRESHOLD` | `float` | `0.6` | At or below this, an answer is held for review, and a held answer never shows a higher score. |
| `CHUNK_SIZE` | `int` | `1200` | 1200, not the 1800 this carried while Markdown tables still held Docling's alignment padding. De-padding changed what the number buys: at 1800 a chunk held 1,118 characters of content instead of 950, the corpus became coarser than the retriever was tuned for, and measured accuracy fell 4.4 points. 1200 restores the granularity and still holds more content than 1800 did. |
| `CHUNK_OVERLAP` | `int` | `150` |  |
| `MAX_EXPANDED_CHARS` | `int` | `12000` |  |
| `MAX_EXPANDED_PARTS` | `int` | `6` | Expansion completes a split unit so the drafter never sees three items of a nine-item series and calls it the list. That is right for a clause series; it is wrong for a chapter. 79% of units in this corpus are a single chunk and 96% are six parts or fewer, but the remaining few run to 40, 100, even 113 parts — a whole standard with no internal headings to divide on. Expanding one of those filled all fourteen prompt slots from a single document and pushed every other policy out. Above this many parts the hit is returned on its own, which is not contextless: every part repeats the unit's stem. |
| `MAX_EVIDENCE_CHUNKS` | `int` | `38` | Cap on accumulated evidence per question. 38 rather than 30 because the smaller chunks above put less text in each slot: at 30 the drafter saw about a fifth less material than before, and four documents per run were retrieved and then cut before reaching it. |
| `MAX_PRIOR_ANSWER_CHUNKS` | `int` | `4` | How many of those chunks may be previous answers. They sort first, so without a ceiling they take the whole prompt and the policies that actually answer the question never reach the drafter — see `select_evidence`. Raise it for a corpus where the previous answers are the authority; lower it to make the drafter lean on the guidelines. |
| `EVIDENCE_SCORE_FLOOR` | `float` | `0.0` | Keep a retrieved unit only if it scores within this fraction of the best hit for the question, so a simple lookup is answered from six chunks and a synthesis question still gets forty. 0 disables it and the budget alone decides. Judged on the agreement-weighted score, so a clause several independent searches converged on survives a floor that its raw cosine would not — the two precision signals available for free, combined. Set it high or not at all: BGE-M3 cosines on policy prose bunch tightly, and on this corpus the median retrieved chunk still scores 94% of the best hit, so anything below ~0.90 discards nothing. |
| `MIN_EVIDENCE_CHUNKS` | `int` | `8` | Never prune below this many chunks, whatever the floor says. A question whose best hit is itself weak would otherwise be answered from one chunk. |
| `RELEVANCE_FILTER_ENABLED` | `bool` | `False` | Grade each retrieved chunk against the question with an LLM, and use the verdicts to re-order the evidence. Cosine cannot do this job on policy prose: even the five best-ranked chunks are only about a third on-target, and every threshold tried on the score itself cost two to four points of recall for each point of precision. A grader reads query and chunk together, which is the interaction an embedding discards. |
| `RELEVANCE_FILTER_BATCH` | `int` | `12` | Chunks per grading call. One call per chunk would be ~2,000 calls for a 42-question run and trips Groq's rate limit; a dozen per call makes it three calls per question, issued concurrently. |
| `RELEVANCE_FILTER_KEEP` | `int` | `8` | Chunks always kept regardless of the verdicts. The grader is one more thing that can be wrong, and a false negative on the only chunk carrying the answer leaves nothing to recover from. |
| `RELEVANCE_FILTER_MODEL` | `str` | `""` | Blank uses GROQ_CHAT_MODEL. A smaller model is faster and cheaper, but verify it on Arabic before trusting it: this corpus is half Arabic, and small models degrade there first. |
| `RELEVANCE_FILTER_SNIPPET` | `int` | `700` | Characters of each chunk shown to the grader. Enough to judge relevance, short enough that a dozen fit in one call. |
| `RELEVANCE_FILTER_PROMOTE` | `bool` | `True` | Move graded-relevant material to the front, rather than only deleting off-target material from the back. Without this the grader can never put a good chunk sitting at position 25 into the top eight -- and the drafter cites about eight sources however many it is shown, so the back of the prompt is the one place a change cannot matter. The keep floor still protects those chunks from deletion; it no longer pins them in place. |
| `QUERY_AGREEMENT_WEIGHT` | `float` | `0.15` | How much a chunk gains for each extra search that independently returned it. Query expansion runs several deliberately overlapping searches per question, so agreement between them is a relevance signal that costs nothing extra to collect. A chunk found by 3 of 4 searches is scored `1 + 2 * weight` times its similarity. 0 disables it; with query expansion off it has no effect either way. See graph/state.py. |
| `EXTRACTION_WINDOW` | `int` | `2000` |  |
| `INCOMPLETE_LIST_CONFIDENCE_CAP` | `float` | `0.5` |  |
| `LOG_LEVEL` | `Literal["DEBUG", "INFO", "WARNING", "ERROR", "CRITICAL"]` | `"INFO"` |  |
| `LOG_FORMAT` | `str` | `"text"` | How log lines are written: "text" for a person at a terminal, "json" for one object per line where a log collector reads them (src/logs.py). |

## Identity and history (Phase 0)

| Variable | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `DB_PATH` | `Path` | `PROJECT_ROOT / "data" / "app.db"` | One SQLite file holds users, teams, sessions, the event log and answered runs. SQLite rather than a server because the whole point of this store is that it is always there: no second process to start, no connection string to get wrong, and a single file to copy when someone wants a backup. |
| `ORGANISATION_PATH` | `Path` | `PROJECT_ROOT / "data" / "organisation.json"` | Who this deployment answers on behalf of (src/organisation.py): a JSON file an administrator edits; when it is missing, the built-in profile is used. |
| `SERVER_LOG_PATH` | `Path` | `PROJECT_ROOT / "logs" / "server.log"` | Where serve.sh writes the server's output; `python -m src.cli inspect request` reads it. |
| `ALLOWED_EMAILS` | `str` | `""` | Members to create on a FIRST run only, comma-separated. Access is administered on the admin page once the system is running -- this exists so a deployment that predates the admin page keeps working, and so a new one can start with its team already listed. Removing someone on the page is not undone by a restart. A plain string rather than `list[str]` deliberately: pydantic-settings tries to JSON-decode list-typed fields, so `ALLOWED_EMAILS=a@t2.sa,b@t2.sa` raises a parse error instead of doing the obvious thing. Read `allowed_emails_set`, never this. |
| `SEED_PRODUCTS` | `str` | `""` | Products added to the default team the first time the server starts, comma-separated. Applied once: the Products page is authoritative after that, so a product deleted there stays deleted (plan 020). |
| `ADMIN_EMAIL` | `str` | `""` | The break-glass administrator, re-applied at every startup. This is the one account the environment owns, and the way back in when a password is lost or the last admin is removed by accident -- so it is also the only account whose password cannot be changed from the admin page. Create a second admin there for everyday use. |
| `ADMIN_PASSWORD` | `str` | `""` |  |
| `SIGN_IN_MAX_ATTEMPTS` | `int` | `10` | A shared access code is only as strong as the number of guesses allowed against it. Counted per address, because the code is shared by a team and an attacker with a proxy pool would otherwise spread guesses across it. |
| `SIGN_IN_LOCKOUT_MINUTES` | `int` | `15` |  |
| `DEFAULT_TEAM` | `str` | `"cybersecurity"` | Everyone who signs in joins this team until there is a reason to have two. Teams exist in the schema from the start because retrofitting a tenant column onto rows that already exist is the migration nobody enjoys. |
| `SESSION_TTL_DAYS` | `int` | `30` | How long a sign-in lasts. Sessions are rows, so this is also how long a revoked-by-deletion session stays revoked. |
